vignette:
Captain's Watch

Marcus has been commanding vessels for nearly twenty years, and the sea has always been his sanctuary. At forty-two, he carries himself with the quiet authority of someone accustomed to making decisions that affect dozens of lives. His weathered hands and sun-deepened skin speak to a career spent largely on the water. He is married to Patricia, a high school teacher who has learned to manage the long stretches of his absence with practiced grace. They have no children—a choice Marcus made early on, wanting to keep his focus where it needed to be: on his crew and his ship.

Three years ago, everything shifted.

Marcus was commanding a mid-sized cargo vessel in the North Atlantic when a catastrophic engine failure occurred during a severe storm. The malfunction cascaded into a series of system failures that he could not have anticipated or prevented. Within hours, the ship began taking on water. Marcus coordinated the evacuation of his crew with methodical precision, ensuring every person made it safely to lifeboats. He was the last to leave the bridge, watching his vessel sink into the dark water as the helicopter lifted him away. No lives were lost. By every objective measure, he had done his job perfectly.

But Marcus cannot shake the feeling that he failed.

Since that night, his world has contracted. He remains hypervigilant, constantly scanning for threats that might emerge without warning. Loud noises—the slam of a door, a car backfiring, even Patricia's blender in the morning—send his heart racing. He finds himself holding his breath, his body tensing as though bracing for impact. These moments are brief, but they leave him exhausted.

Sleep has become unreliable. Most nights, Marcus lies awake beside Patricia, his mind replaying the sequence of events with painful clarity. When sleep finally comes, he is back on that bridge, watching the instruments fail one by one, feeling the helplessness rise in his chest like the water rising in the hull. He wakes gasping, sometimes finding himself on the floor before he realizes where he is. Patricia has learned not to touch him during these episodes; it only startles him further.

The shipping company offered him a promotion to a desk position. Marcus declined. The thought of returning to sea terrifies him, but the thought of leaving it feels like a death of another kind. Instead, he finds himself in a painful limbo—unable to captain a ship, unable to accept that he cannot. He has taken leave from work, telling Patricia he needs time to think, though they both know it is more complicated than that.

He avoids conversations about the incident, even with Patricia, though she has gently asked if he would consider talking to someone. He nods and says maybe, but the words feel hollow. Part of him believes that discussing it would somehow make it more real, would transform the memory into something he cannot contain.

What troubles Marcus most is not the memories themselves, but the way they have colonized his present. He watches Patricia move through their home and feels a profound distance between them, as though he is observing her life from behind glass. He used to love the smell of salt water and diesel fuel. Now, he cannot bear to walk near the harbor. The man who once felt most alive on the open ocean now finds himself afraid of the very thing that defined him.
